notes:
I found notes for every verse, but the research is incomplete in ways that matter for your second goal. My search tool hit its usage limit partway through, so I couldn't find Methodist/Wesleyan, Lutheran, Pentecostal, Anglican, Orthodox or Bible Odyssey sources, or any prosperity, word-of-faith or hyper-grace teaching on Jonah 4. Most of the sources below are Reformed or Calvinist (Calvin, Gill, Ligonier, Matthew Henry, Geneva) or general evangelical. Two other caveats: some Bible Hub notes appear on the page without a commentator's name, so I credit those to "Bible Hub" rather than guess an author. And on Enduring Word I used only Guzik's own commentary, not the AI-written summary at the top of the page.

---

## v. 1: Jonah's anger

**Traditional reading**
- Jonah is angry because God spared the Ninevites. They were Assyrians, enemies of Israel and Judah, and he wanted them judged. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/jonah-4/
- Gill calls Jonah a very strange man: a good man and a prophet who was upset by the very thing that should have delighted him, the success of his preaching. He had also just been rescued from the fish himself. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/jonah-4.html
- Gill weighs several possible reasons and finds them all weak: worry about being called a false prophet, the honour of his own country, prejudice against Gentiles, and concern for God's glory. He compares Jonah to the Jews in Acts who tried to stop the apostles preaching to Gentiles. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/jonah/4-1.html
- Matthew Henry traces the anger to pride and wounded honour. Jonah was jealous for Israel's honour, since Nineveh's repentance shamed unrepentant Israel. Henry calls this zeal for God "not according to knowledge" and compares Peter's first reluctance about the Gentiles. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Jon/Jon_004.cfm
- GotQuestions gives three reasons: Jonah would rather have seen Nineveh destroyed, he wanted his sense of justice satisfied, and sparing the city could make his prophecy look false. https://www.gotquestions.org/Jonah-angry.html

## v. 2: "I knew that You are a gracious and compassionate God…"

**Traditional reading**
- Jonah now admits why he ran away. He wasn't afraid of failing; he was afraid of succeeding. Guzik notes that Jonah had relied on God's mercy for himself but resented it reaching others. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/jonah-4/
- Gill calls this a disorderly prayer made in a fit of temper, very different from his prayer inside the fish. Jonah even justifies his flight, as if he had seen things more clearly than God. Gill takes this as a lesson that God's discipline restrains sin in good people but does not remove it completely. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/jonah-4.html
- Calvin says God still treated this as a real prayer, even though Jonah prayed wrongly and boasted of running away. Calvin thinks Jonah felt he had been made to look false, and that he still held to the truth that God "cannot divest himself of his mercy." https://www.studylight.org/commentary/jonah/4-2.html
- Matthew Henry calls it "a very awkward prayer": Jonah complains about the mercy others received instead of asking for it himself. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Jon/Jon_004.cfm

**Modern scholarship (NET Bible notes)**
- In chapter 3 the same Hebrew verb, *shub*, is used for the Ninevites "repenting" and for God "relenting". The wordplay shows God's response was fitting: they turned from their evil, so he turned from the disaster. The NET notes say this verse is the first place the narrator reveals why Jonah fled in 1:3: he didn't want to give God the chance to relent. https://classic.net.bible.org/passage.php?passage=Jon+3%3A9-10%3B4%3A2

**How teachers explain "relents from sending disaster"**
- Reformed (Ligonier): God's mind cannot change, because everything falls within his unchanging decree. Verses that speak of God "relenting" (Jonah 3:10 is cited) describe a change in how he deals with people, not in his inner purpose. They are read non-literally, much like verses that give God eyes or ears. https://learn.ligonier.org/articles/does-god-change-his-mind
- R.C. Sproul (Ligonier) says this was exactly Jonah's complaint. He insists that when God holds back a threatened judgment after repentance, the unchangeable God has not changed. https://learn.ligonier.org/podcasts/ultimately-with-rc-sproul/does-god-repent
- General evangelical (GotQuestions): the threat to Nineveh was conditional, a warning meant to bring repentance, as Jeremiah 18:7–11 describes. So God did not change his mind; he acted consistently. https://www.gotquestions.org/God-change-mind.html

## v. 3: "Take my life"

- Guzik: Nineveh's salvation hurt Jonah so much that he would rather die. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/jonah-4/
- Gill: Jonah was right to see life as God's to take, and he did not try to end it himself. Still, he was wrong to ask. He was in no fit state to die, quarrelling with God and lacking love for God or for people. Gill also reports Aben Ezra's and Kimchi's view that Jonah didn't want to live to see the harm he feared Nineveh's repentance would bring on Israel. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/jonah-4.html
- Matthew Henry calls Jonah a melancholy man who imagined troubles that were never likely to happen. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Jon/Jon_004.cfm

## v. 4: "Have you any right to be angry?"

- Guzik: Jonah was right to be honest with God about his anger, but not every feeling toward God is justified, and Jonah needed to repent of it. This question exposes the real problem. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/jonah-4/
- Gill calls it a gentle rebuke that shows the very slowness to anger Jonah complained about. God could have struck him dead, as with Ananias and Sapphira. Gill stresses the "thou": a creature, a prophet who had just been shown mercy, angry with his Creator. He also mentions another reading, "Is doing good displeasing to you?", and compares the Pharisees and the prodigal son's older brother. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/jonah-4.html

## v. 5: The shelter east of the city

**Traditional reading**
- Matthew Henry: Jonah stayed close by, as if he expected and wanted the city's overthrow. Fretful people make trouble for themselves. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/jonah/4-5.htm
- Poole: Jonah was discontented and unsure how things would turn out. The east side was probably higher ground, safer and with a better view. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/jonah/4-5.htm
- Coffman (Restoration Movement): the east side gave the best view of the destruction Jonah hoped for. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/jonah/4-5.html

**When did Jonah leave? (a real disagreement)**
- Barnes: Jonah left after he was convinced God would spare the city, probably once the 40 days were over, though he still hoped for some punishment. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/jonah/4-5.htm
- Clarke: he left right after preaching and waited, and his anger came after the 40 days passed without judgment. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/jonah/4-5.html
- Gill mentions a translation, "Jonah *had* gone out", which would place this verse before the events of verses 1–4. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/jonah-4.html
- Jamieson-Fausset-Brown (JFB): the 40 days were not over. Jonah wasn't sulking; he didn't know whether Nineveh's punishment had been cancelled or only put off. God made the shelter "a school of discipline". https://biblehub.com/commentaries/jonah/4-5.htm

## v. 6: The plant

**Traditional reading**
- Guzik: as God prepared the fish, he now prepares the plant. This is the first time Jonah is happy, and that happiness is as self-centred as his anger. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/jonah-4/
- Gill: Jonah may have taken the plant as a sign God approved of him. We should be thankful for outward blessings, but not overjoyed by them. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/jonah-4.html
- Matthew Henry: a small thing that comes at the right time can be a real blessing. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/jonah/4-5.htm

**What kind of plant?**
- The Hebrew word is *kikayon*, used only here in the Old Testament. Commentaries on Bible Hub record that the Greek Old Testament (Septuagint) has "gourd" and the Latin Vulgate "ivy". Several, including JFB, identify it as the castor-oil plant (*ricinus*). One unnamed note cites Tristram, who leaned toward the bottle gourd because gourds were commonly grown to shade arbours. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/jonah/4-6.htm
- Clarke prefers the castor-oil plant and translates "the Lord *had* prepared": the plant had already grown there by God's providence. Coffman rejects the castor-bean explanation and treats the growth as a miracle. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/jonah/4-6.html
- Calvin calls the dispute unimportant and would keep "gourd" rather than cause a disturbance. He thinks the growth was extraordinary, and that the plant sheltered Jonah together with the booth he had built. https://ccel.org/ccel/calvin/calcom28/calcom28.iii.4.viii.html

**Early church (Catholic and Orthodox heritage)**
- Jerome explains why he translated "ivy": the Hebrew names a self-supporting shrub with no exact Latin word. His new rendering had caused an uproar in one church. https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/1102075.htm
- Augustine replies that he would still keep "gourd" in Latin Bibles, trusting the Septuagint translators. https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/1102082.htm
- Augustine also reads the plant as a picture of the Old Testament promises and privileges, a "shadow of things to come." https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/1102102.htm

## v. 7: The worm

- Augustine sees the "morning worm" as a picture of Christ, using Psalm 22's "I am a worm". The gospel caused Israel's shadowy privileges to wither, and Jonah scorched by the sun pictures Israel scattered in exile. https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/1102102.htm
- Gill reports Jerome's similar allegory (the plant as the ceremonial law, the worm as Christ). Gill prefers to apply it to earthly comforts, which are thin and quickly gone. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/jonah/4-6.htm
- Chuck Smith (Calvary Chapel) notes the repeated "God prepared/appointed": fish, plant, worm and wind. God controls the whole scene. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/jonah/4-4.html

## v. 8: The east wind

- Matthew Henry: sometimes the thing we have stays but the comfort is taken out of it. When our "gourd" is gone, our God is not gone. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/jonah/4-5.htm
- Guzik: the real thing God was preparing was the prophet himself. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/jonah-4/

## v. 9: "I am angry enough to die!"

- Guzik: these are Jonah's last recorded words, but thankfully not the last words of the book. God's mercy keeps working on him. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/jonah-4/
- Gill points out that God mentions only the plant, not the wind and sun, because the plant would have protected Jonah from both. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/jonah/4-9.html

## v. 10: "You cared about the plant…"

- Smith: the plant was short-lived, and Jonah did nothing to plant it, water it or make it grow. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/jonah/4-6.html
- Bridgeway: Jonah felt sorry for a plant he didn't make that lasted one day. How much more should God feel for people he made? https://www.studylight.org/commentary/jonah/4-2.html
- One unnamed note on Bible Hub argues that God has far more right to pity creatures he made and kept alive than Jonah had to pity a shrub. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/jonah/4-11.htm

## v. 11: "Should I not care about the great city of Nineveh…?"

**Who "cannot tell their right hand from their left"?**
- Young children: JFB says children under three or four (compare Deuteronomy 1:39) and estimates a total population of about 600,000. The Geneva Bible notes also say children and infants. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/jonah/4-11.htm
- Smith also reads it as little children, and says God spared the city partly for the animals. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/jonah/4-11.html
- Guzik takes it differently: people unable to make moral judgments. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/jonah-4/

**God's care for animals**
- JFB: God cares even for animals that people take little account of. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/jonah/4-11.htm
- Kelly: true greatness takes in the small things along with the vast. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/jonah/4-11.html

**The book's point**
- Guzik: God cares for people beyond Israel, all made in his image, and Jonah didn't know God as well as he thought. He links this to Jonah 2:9 ("Salvation is of the LORD") and Acts 10:34–35. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/jonah-4/
- A quotation in the Light of Israel commentary (from Phillips) says Jonah didn't know God well enough to grieve over sin, or rejoice over repentance, the way God does. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/jonah/4-11.html
- Matthew Henry: people who want to keep God's grace for their own group will learn there is one Lord over all, rich in mercy to everyone who calls on him. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/jonah/4-5.htm
